questionText: Which triangle can have angles 48° and 66°?
hints: The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. Find the missing angle, then look at all three to name the triangle.
Add 48° and 66°, and take the total away from 180° to get the third angle.
Similar example: a triangle has angles 35° and 55°. 35 + 55 = 90, and 180 − 90 = 90. The third angle is 90°, a right angle, so it is a right-angled triangle.

stepByStep.text: Add the two angles you know.
Take this from 180° to get the third angle.
The angles are 48°, 66° and 66°. Two of them are equal.
A triangle with two equal angles has two equal sides. So it is an Isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60° each. Here the angles are 48°, 66° and 66°.
misconceptions.B: A right-angled triangle needs one angle of 90°. Here the third angle is 66°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The third angle is 66°, so two angles are equal and the triangle is isosceles.
misconceptions.D: An obtuse-angled triangle needs one angle bigger than 90°. Here every angle is less than 90°.

questionText: Which angles CANNOT be triangle angles?
hints: The three angles of any triangle add up to exactly 180°. Add each set and look for the one that does not make 180°.
Start with the first set: add 70, 60 and 40. Then do the same for the other sets.
Similar example: can 50°, 65° and 55° be the angles of a triangle? 50 + 65 + 55 = 170, which is not 180, so they cannot. Can 50°, 65° and 65°? 50 + 65 + 65 = 180, so they can.

stepByStep.text: Add the first set.
This total is 10° short of 180°, so these cannot be the angles of a triangle.
The other three sets each add up to 180°: 75 + 55 + 50 = 180, 45 + 45 + 90 = 180 and 30 + 80 + 70 = 180.
So the angles that cannot make a triangle are 70°, 60°, 40°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 70 + 60 + 40 = 170, which is not 180, so no triangle can have these angles.
misconceptions.B: 75 + 55 + 50 = 180, so these can be the angles of a triangle. Look for the set that does not add up to 180.
misconceptions.C: 45 + 45 + 90 = 180, so these can be the angles of a triangle. Look for the set that does not add up to 180.
misconceptions.D: 30 + 80 + 70 = 180, so these can be the angles of a triangle. Look for the set that does not add up to 180.

questionText: Triangle BED has a base of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is the area of triangle BED?
hints: The area of a triangle is half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height.
Multiply the base by the height: 6 × 4. Then remember that a triangle takes up only half of that.
Similar example: a triangle has base 10 cm and height 3 cm. 10 × 3 = 30, and half of 30 is 15, so the area is 15 sq cm.

stepByStep.text: Multiply the base by the height.
A triangle is half of that rectangle, so divide by 2.
The area of triangle BED is 12 sq.cm.

misconceptions.A: 6 cm is the length of the base. Area needs base times height, then half of that, and it is measured in square centimetres.
misconceptions.B: Area is measured in square centimetres, not centimetres. Work out half of 6 × 4.
misconceptions.C: 24 is base times height, which is the area of the whole rectangle. A triangle is half of that.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Half of 6 × 4 is 12, so the area is 12 square centimetres.

questionText: Right triangle base=19cm, height=16cm. Area?
hints: The area of a right triangle is half the area of the rectangle with the same base and height. Watch the unit too.
Multiply the base by the height first. Then remember that the triangle takes up only half of that.
Similar example: a right triangle has base 14 cm and height 10 cm. 14 × 10 = 140, and half of 140 is 70. Its area is 70 cm.sq.

stepByStep.text: Multiply the base by the height.
The triangle is half of this rectangle.
The sides are in centimetres, so the area is 152 cm.sq.

misconceptions.A: The number is right, but look at the unit. The sides are in centimetres, so the area is in square centimetres, not square metres.
misconceptions.B: Check the multiplication. 19 × 16 = 304, and half of 304 is a little more than this.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Half of 19 × 16 is 152, and the unit is square centimetres.
misconceptions.D: This is base times height, the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of it.

questionText: Which pair can be isosceles triangle angles?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. Use the fact that all three angles add up to 180° to find the third angle of each pair.
For the first pair, add 63 and 54 and take the total from 180. See whether the third angle matches one of the two given.
Similar example: can 50° and 80° be two angles of an isosceles triangle? 50 + 80 = 130, and 180 − 130 = 50. The third angle is 50°, the same as one already there, so yes.

stepByStep.text: Add the first pair.
Find the third angle.
The angles are 63°, 54° and 63°. Two are equal, so this triangle is isosceles.
The other pairs give third angles of 60°, 51° and 68°, which match nothing in their pairs.
So the pair is 63°, 54°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The third angle is 180 − 117 = 63, which matches the 63° already there.
misconceptions.B: 75 + 45 = 120, so the third angle is 60°. All three angles are different, so it is not isosceles.
misconceptions.C: 49 + 80 = 129, so the third angle is 51°. That is close to 49° but not equal.
misconceptions.D: 59 + 53 = 112, so the third angle is 68°. All three angles are different, so it is not isosceles.

questionText: Two sides of triangle = 20cm and 15cm. Which CANNOT be perimeter?
hints: In any triangle, two sides together must be longer than the third side. Use this to see how long the third side can be.
Add the two sides you know, 20 and 15. The third side must be shorter than this total. Then find the third side for each perimeter.

Similar example: two sides of a triangle are 10 cm and 8 cm. 10 + 8 = 18, so the third side must be shorter than 18 cm. Can the perimeter be 40 cm? The third side would be 40 − 18 = 22 cm, which is too long. So 40 cm is not possible.

stepByStep.text: Add the two sides you know.
The third side must be shorter than 35 cm, or the two sides could not reach across it.
So the perimeter must be less than 70 cm.
For a perimeter of 72 cm the third side would be 37 cm, which is too long.
So the perimeter cannot be 72cm.

misconceptions.A: 52 − 35 = 17, so the third side would be 17 cm. That is shorter than 35 cm, so this triangle can be made.
misconceptions.B: 67 − 35 = 32, so the third side would be 32 cm. That is shorter than 35 cm, so this triangle can be made.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The third side would be 72 − 35 = 37 cm, longer than the other two sides put together.
misconceptions.D: 62 − 35 = 27, so the third side would be 27 cm. That is shorter than 35 cm, so this triangle can be made.

questionText: Which pair of angles can be two angles of isosceles triangle?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. Use the fact that all three angles add up to 180° to find the third angle of each pair.
For each pair, add the two angles and take the total from 180. See whether the third angle matches one of the two given.
Similar example: can 70° and 40° be two angles of an isosceles triangle? 70 + 40 = 110, and 180 − 110 = 70. The third angle is 70°, the same as one already there, so yes.

stepByStep.text: Try the pair 68° and 44°. Add them.
Find the third angle.
The angles are 68°, 44° and 68°. Two are equal, so this triangle is isosceles.
The other pairs give third angles of 57.5° and 63°, which match nothing in their pairs.
So the pair is 68° & 44°.

misconceptions.A: 64 + 58.5 = 122.5, so the third angle is 57.5°. That is close to 58.5° but not equal.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The third angle is 180 − 112 = 68, which matches the 68° already there.
misconceptions.C: 62.5 + 54.5 = 117, so the third angle is 63°. That is close to 62.5° but not equal.
misconceptions.D: One pair does work. Find the third angle for 68° and 44° and compare it with them.

questionText: Which base and height of triangle gives area = square of side 9cm?
hints: Find the area of the square first. Then find the area of each triangle and look for the one that matches.
The square has side 9 cm, so its area is 9 × 9. A triangle's area is half of its base times its height.
Similar example: a square has side 4 cm, so its area is 4 × 4 = 16 sq cm. A triangle with base 8 cm and height 4 cm has 8 × 4 = 32, and half of 32 is 16 sq cm. The two areas are equal.

stepByStep.text: Find the area of the square.
A triangle's area is half of base times height. So base times height must be twice 81, which is 162.
Check base 27 and height 6.
Half of 162 is the triangle's area.
So the triangle with B=27, H=6 has the same area as the square.

misconceptions.A: Half of 12 × 4 is 24. The square's area is 9 × 9 = 81, so this triangle is too small.
misconceptions.B: Half of 18 × 8 is 72. That is close, but the square's area is 9 × 9 = 81.
misconceptions.C: Half of 12 × 14 is 84. That is close, but the square's area is 9 × 9 = 81.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Half of 27 × 6 is 81, the same as 9 × 9.

questionText: The sum of all angles of a triangle is:
hints: This is a fact about every triangle, whatever its shape. Think about what you get when you put its three corners together.
Picture tearing the three corners off a paper triangle and placing them side by side. They fit along a straight line. Think how many degrees a straight line makes.
Similar example: think of a rectangle. It has 4 corners, and each is a right angle of 90°. 4 × 90 = 360, so the angles of a rectangle add up to 360°.

stepByStep.text: Put the three corners of any triangle side by side. Together they make a straight line.
A straight line is half of a full turn, and a full turn is 360°.
Half of 360° is the angle on a straight line.
So the sum of all angles of a triangle is 180°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The three angles of any triangle always add up to 180°.
misconceptions.B: 360° is a full turn, and the angle sum of a four-sided shape. A triangle's corners make only a straight line.
misconceptions.C: 90° is one right angle. The three angles of a triangle together make two right angles.
misconceptions.D: 270° is three right angles. The three angles of a triangle together make two right angles.

questionText: A triangle with all sides equal is called:
hints: Triangles get their names from how many of their sides are equal. Think about the names you know.
Rule out the names you are sure about. Scalene means no sides are equal, and isosceles means just two sides are equal.
Similar example: a triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. Exactly two sides are equal, so it is called an isosceles triangle.

stepByStep.text: Triangles are named by their sides. If no sides are equal it is scalene, and if two sides are equal it is isosceles.
When all three sides are equal, the name comes from words meaning equal sides.
A triangle with all sides equal is called Equilateral.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Equilateral means equal sides, and all three sides are the same length.
misconceptions.B: An isosceles triangle has only two equal sides. Here all three sides are equal.
misconceptions.C: A scalene triangle has no equal sides at all. Here all three sides are equal.
misconceptions.D: Right-angled tells us about an angle of 90°, not about the sides. Look for the name that means equal sides.

questionText: A triangle with two equal sides is called:
hints: Triangles get their names from how many of their sides are equal. Think about the names you know.
Rule out the names you are sure about. Scalene means no sides are equal, and equilateral means all three sides are equal.
Similar example: a triangle has sides 4 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. No two sides are equal, so it is called a scalene triangle.

stepByStep.text: Triangles are named by their sides. If no sides are equal it is scalene, and if all three are equal it is equilateral.
The name for exactly two equal sides comes from words meaning equal legs.
A triangle with two equal sides is called Isosceles.

misconceptions.A: Yes! An isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides.
misconceptions.B: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Here only two sides are equal.
misconceptions.C: A scalene triangle has no equal sides. Here two sides are equal.
misconceptions.D: Obtuse tells us about an angle bigger than 90°, not about the sides. Look for the name that means two equal sides.

questionText: If two angles of a triangle are 50° and 60°, the third angle is:
hints: The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. Two are given, so find what is left for the third.
First add the two angles you know, 50° and 60°. Then think about how far that total is from 180°.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 40° and 65°. 40 + 65 = 105, and 180 − 105 = 75. The third angle is 75°.

stepByStep.text: Add the two angles you know.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Take the total away from 180°. The third angle is 70°.

misconceptions.B: This is 10° too big. The two angles add up to 110°, so take 110 from 180 once more.
misconceptions.C: A triangle does not need a 90° angle. Add 50 and 60, then take the total from 180.
misconceptions.D: 60° is one of the angles already given. Add 50 and 60, then take the total from 180.

questionText: A triangle with one angle 90° is called:
hints: Triangles can also be named by their biggest angle. Think about the special name for an angle of 90°.
Rule out the names you are sure about. Acute means every angle is less than 90°, and obtuse means one angle is more than 90°.
Similar example: a triangle has angles 30°, 40° and 110°. One angle is more than 90°, so it is called an obtuse-angled triangle.

stepByStep.text: An angle of exactly 90° is called a right angle. It looks like the corner of a book.
A triangle is named after its biggest angle: acute if all are less than 90°, obtuse if one is more than 90°.
A triangle with one angle of 90° is called Right-angled.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A 90° angle is a right angle, so the triangle is right-angled.
misconceptions.B: In an acute triangle every angle is less than 90°. Here one angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.C: An obtuse triangle has one angle more than 90°. Here the angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.D: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°. It can never have a 90° angle.

questionText: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. What kind of triangle is it?

options.text: These sides cannot make a triangle

hints: Triangles are named by how many of their sides are equal. Compare the three lengths.
Two of the lengths are 5 cm and the third is 8 cm. How many sides are equal?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 7 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm has three different lengths, so it is a scalene triangle.

stepByStep.text: The two shorter sides together are 10 cm, which is more than 8 cm, so the sides do make a triangle.
Exactly two sides are equal: 5 cm and 5 cm.
A triangle with exactly two equal sides is an isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Here the third side is 8 cm, not 5 cm.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Two sides are 5 cm and the third is different, so it is isosceles.
misconceptions.C: A scalene triangle has three different sides. Here two of the sides are the same.
misconceptions.D: The two shorter sides add up to 10 cm, which is more than 8 cm, so they do close up into a triangle.

questionText: The angles of a triangle are 35°, 55° and 90°. What kind of triangle is it?
hints: Triangles can be named by their biggest angle. Is it less than 90°, exactly 90°, or more than 90°?
The biggest of the three angles is 90°. What is an angle of 90° called?
A similar one: a triangle with angles 30°, 40° and 110° has one angle bigger than 90°, so it is an obtuse-angled triangle.

stepByStep.text: The biggest angle is 90°.
An angle of 90° is a right angle.
A triangle with one right angle is a right-angled triangle.

misconceptions.A: In an acute-angled triangle all three angles are less than 90°. Here one angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.B: An obtuse-angled triangle has one angle more than 90°. Here the biggest angle is exactly 90°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! One angle is 90°, a right angle.
misconceptions.D: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60° each. These three angles are all different.

questionText: All three sides of a triangle have different lengths. By its sides, what is the triangle called?
hints: There are three names for triangles by their sides: one for three equal sides, one for two equal sides, and one for no equal sides.
This triangle has no two sides the same. Which of the three names is for that?
A similar one: a triangle with sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm has all sides equal, so it is called an equilateral triangle.

stepByStep.text: Three equal sides make an equilateral triangle, and two equal sides make an isosceles triangle.
This triangle has no equal sides at all.
A triangle with three different sides is a scalene triangle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Scalene means no two sides are equal.
misconceptions.B: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. Here all three are different.
misconceptions.C: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides. Here all three are different.
misconceptions.D: Right-angled is a name that comes from the angles. The question asks for the name that comes from the sides.

questionText: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of 9 cm each. Its third side is 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
hints: The perimeter is the distance all the way around, so add all three sides.
The three sides are 9 cm, 9 cm and 6 cm. Add them.
A similar one: equal sides of 5 cm each and a third side of 4 cm give a perimeter of 5 + 5 + 4 = 14 cm.

stepByStep.text: The three sides are 9 cm, 9 cm and 6 cm.
Add them.
The perimeter is 24 cm.

misconceptions.A: 15 cm adds 9 and 6 only. There are two sides of 9 cm.
misconceptions.B: 21 cm uses one side of 9 cm and two of 6 cm. It is the 9 cm side that comes twice.
misconceptions.C: 54 comes from multiplying 9 by 6. For perimeter, add the three sides.

questionText: A triangle has angles 100°, 40° and 40°. Which name describes it best?
hints: The name has two parts. One part comes from the biggest angle. The other part comes from how many angles, and so how many sides, are equal.
The biggest angle is 100°. Is that less than, equal to, or more than 90°? Then look at the two angles of 40°.
A similar one: a triangle with angles 90°, 45° and 45° has a right angle and two equal angles, so it is a right-angled isosceles triangle.

stepByStep.text: The biggest angle is 100°, which is more than 90°, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
Two angles are equal, both 40°. The sides opposite equal angles are equal, so two sides are equal.
It is an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: Acute-angled means every angle is less than 90°. Here one angle is 100°.
misconceptions.B: Scalene means no sides are equal. Two equal angles give two equal sides.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 100° makes it obtuse-angled, and the two angles of 40° make it isosceles.
misconceptions.D: Right-angled needs an angle of exactly 90°. The biggest angle here is 100°.

questionText: Which of these sets of lengths cannot be the sides of a triangle?
hints: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are longer than the longest one.
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the total with the longest length. Watch for a total that is only equal, not greater.
A similar one: 2 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm cannot make a triangle, because 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 7 and the short sides cannot meet.

stepByStep.text: 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 5, and 6 + 6 = 12 is more than 11. These two sets make triangles.
7 + 8 = 15 is more than 14, so this set makes a triangle too.
4 + 5 = 9 is only equal to the longest side, 9. The two short sides would lie flat along the long side.
The set that cannot make a triangle is 4 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 5, so these lengths do make a triangle.
misconceptions.B: 6 + 6 = 12 is more than 11, so these lengths do make a triangle, a rather flat one.
misconceptions.C: 7 + 8 = 15 is more than 14, so these lengths do make a triangle.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 4 + 5 is exactly 9, so the two short sides cannot rise above the long side to form a triangle.

questionText: In a right-angled triangle, one of the two acute angles is twice the other. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. In a right-angled triangle one angle is 90°, so think about what is left for the other two.
The two acute angles together make 90°. One is twice the other, so think of them as 1 part and 2 parts.
A similar one: in a right-angled triangle one acute angle is 4 times the other. Five equal parts make 90°, so one part is 18°. The angles are 18° and 72°, and the smallest is 18°.

stepByStep.text: The two acute angles together.
One angle is 1 part and the other is 2 parts, so 3 parts make 90°.
The acute angles are 30° and 60°.
The smallest angle is 30°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°, and 60° is twice 30°.
misconceptions.B: 60° is the bigger of the two acute angles. The question asks for the smallest angle.
misconceptions.C: 45° would make the two acute angles equal. One of them must be twice the other.
misconceptions.D: 15° comes from sharing 90° into too many parts. One part and two parts make 3 parts in all.

questionText: The perimeter of an isosceles triangle is 40 cm. The side that is different from the other two is 12 cm. How long is each of the equal sides?
hints: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides. Take away the side you know, and what is left belongs to the two equal sides.
Take 12 cm away from 40 cm. The rest is shared equally between the two equal sides.
A similar one: perimeter 26 cm and a different side of 6 cm. The two equal sides share 26 − 6 = 20 cm, so each is 10 cm.

stepByStep.text: Take the different side away from the perimeter.
The two equal sides share this equally.
Each equal side is 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: 28 cm is the two equal sides together. Share it between the two sides.
misconceptions.C: 20 cm is half the perimeter. Take away the 12 cm side before halving.
misconceptions.D: 16 cm comes from taking 12 away twice. The 12 cm side appears only once.

questionText: All three angles of a triangle are equal. What is the sum of any two of its angles?
hints: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°. If they are all equal, you can find one of them.
Share 180° equally among three angles to find each one. Then add two of them.
A similar one: a right-angled triangle has two equal angles. They share 180 − 90 = 90°, so each is 45°, and those two together make 90°.

stepByStep.text: The three equal angles add up to 180°, so find one angle.
Add two of the angles.
The sum of any two angles is 120°.

misconceptions.A: 60° is one angle. The question asks for two of them added together.
misconceptions.B: 180° is the sum of all three angles. Add only two of them.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Each angle is 60°, and 60° + 60° = 120°.
misconceptions.D: 90° would be right for the two equal angles of a right-angled triangle. Here each angle is 60°.

questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 7 cm and 10 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the greatest length the third side can have?
hints: In a triangle, any two sides together must be longer than the third side. Use this to find how long the third side is allowed to be.
Add the two sides you know. The third side must be shorter than this total, not equal to it.
A similar one: with sides 4 cm and 6 cm, the third side must be shorter than 4 + 6 = 10 cm. The greatest whole number is 9 cm.

stepByStep.text: Add the two known sides.
The third side must be shorter than 17 cm. At exactly 17 cm the two sides would lie flat along it.
The greatest whole number less than 17 is 16.
The greatest length of the third side is 16 cm.

misconceptions.A: At 17 cm the other two sides would lie flat along the third side and no triangle would form. It must be a little shorter.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 7 + 10 = 17 is more than 16, so the triangle closes, and 16 is the greatest whole number that fits.
misconceptions.C: 18 cm is longer than the other two sides put together, so they could not reach each other.
misconceptions.D: 3 cm is the difference of the two sides. That is about the shortest end, and the question asks for the greatest length.

questionText: Jay has four sticks of lengths 3 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm. He picks three sticks at a time to make a triangle. How many different triangles can he make?
hints: List every way of choosing three sticks from the four. Then test each choice: the two shorter sticks together must be longer than the longest one.
There are four ways to choose three sticks: leave out one stick each time. Begin with 3, 5 and 7, and compare 3 + 5 with 7.
A similar one: sticks of 1 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. Of the four choices, only 2, 3 and 4 works, because 2 + 3 = 5 is more than 4. So 1 triangle can be made.

stepByStep.text: Sticks 3, 5, 7: 3 + 5 = 8 is more than 7, so this makes a triangle.
Sticks 3, 5, 10: 3 + 5 = 8 is less than 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 3, 7, 10: 3 + 7 = 10 is only equal to 10, so no triangle.
Sticks 5, 7, 10: 5 + 7 = 12 is more than 10, so this makes a triangle.
He can make 2 different triangles.

misconceptions.A: 4 is the number of ways to choose three sticks, but not every choice closes into a triangle. Test each one.
misconceptions.B: 3 counts the sticks 3, 7 and 10 as a triangle. But 3 + 7 is exactly 10, so those sticks would lie flat.
misconceptions.C: There is more than one. Both 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10 pass the test.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Only 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10 make triangles.

questionText: In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the two equal sides is 3 times each of the other two angles. How big is that angle?
hints: In an isosceles triangle the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Think of the angles as equal parts that add up to 180°.
Call each of the two equal angles 1 part. The angle between the equal sides is then 3 parts. How many parts are there altogether?
A similar one: if the top angle is twice each base angle, the angles are 2 parts, 1 part and 1 part. Four parts make 180°, so one part is 45° and the top angle is 90°.

stepByStep.text: The two equal angles are 1 part each, and the angle between the equal sides is 3 parts.
Five parts make 180°, so find one part.
The angle between the equal sides is 3 parts.
That angle is 108°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The angles are 108°, 36° and 36°, which add up to 180°.
misconceptions.B: 36° is each of the two equal angles. The angle asked for is 3 times as big.
misconceptions.C: 135° comes from sharing 180° into 4 parts. There are 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 parts.
misconceptions.D: 60° is the angle when all three angles are equal. Here one angle is 3 times each of the others.

questionText: In a triangle, the second angle is 20° more than the first angle, and the third angle is 20° more than the second. What is the largest angle?
hints: The three angles add up to 180°. Describe the second and third angles by how much more they are than the first.
The second angle is the first plus 20°, and the third is the first plus 40°. So three times the first angle, plus 60°, makes 180°.
A similar one: the second angle is 10° more than the first and the third is 10° more than the second. Three times the first plus 30° is 180°, so the first is 50° and the largest is 70°.

stepByStep.text: The third angle is 20° + 20° = 40° more than the first.
Take the extra 20° and 40° away from 180°. What is left is three times the first angle.
Find the first angle.
The largest angle is the third one.
The largest angle is 80°.

misconceptions.A: 40° is the first, smallest angle. The largest is 40° more than that.
misconceptions.B: 60° is the second, middle angle. The third angle is 20° more.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The angles are 40°, 60° and 80°, which add up to 180°.
misconceptions.D: 100° would make the angles 60°, 80° and 100°, which add up to 240°. The three angles must total 180°.

questionText: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 50 cm. One of its sides is 12 cm long. Which of these can be the lengths of its other two sides?
hints: There are two things to check: two of the three sides must be equal, and the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side.
The 12 cm side could be one of the equal pair, or it could be the side that is different. Work out the sides in each case and test whether they can close into a triangle.
A similar one: an isosceles triangle with perimeter 20 cm and one side 4 cm. Sides 4, 4 and 12 cannot close, because 4 + 4 is less than 12. Sides 4, 8 and 8 can, so the other sides are 8 cm and 8 cm.

stepByStep.text: If 12 cm is one of the equal sides, the sides are 12, 12 and 26.
But 12 + 12 = 24 is less than 26, so those sides cannot close into a triangle.
If 12 cm is the different side, the equal sides share the rest.
Check: 12 + 19 is more than 19, so the triangle closes. The other two sides are 19 cm and 19 cm.

misconceptions.A: These add up to 50 cm with two equal sides, but 12 + 12 = 24 is less than 26, so the sides cannot meet.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 12 + 19 + 19 = 50, two sides are equal, and the triangle closes.
misconceptions.C: These add up to 50 cm, but 12, 14 and 24 are all different, so the triangle would not be isosceles.
misconceptions.D: These add up to 50 cm, but 12, 18 and 20 are all different, so the triangle would not be isosceles.

questionText: Which of these statements about triangles is true?

options.text: A triangle can have two obtuse angles
An equilateral triangle can be right-angled
A scalene triangle can have two equal angles
A right-angled triangle can be isosceles

hints: Test each statement with two facts: the three angles of a triangle add up to 180°, and equal sides sit opposite equal angles.
For each statement, try to write down three angles that would fit it and still add up to 180°. If you cannot, the statement is not true.
A similar test: can a triangle have two right angles? 90° + 90° is already 180°, which leaves nothing for the third angle. So it cannot.

stepByStep.text: Two obtuse angles would add up to more than 180°, so a triangle cannot have them.
An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°, so it never has a right angle.
Two equal angles give two equal sides, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides.
Angles of 90°, 45° and 45° add up to 180° and two of them are equal. So the true statement is: A right-angled triangle can be isosceles.

misconceptions.A: Each obtuse angle is more than 90°, so two of them are already more than 180°. A triangle has room for only one.
misconceptions.B: Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°, so none of them can be 90°.
misconceptions.C: Equal angles always sit opposite equal sides. A scalene triangle has no equal sides, so it has no equal angles.
misconceptions.D: Yes! A triangle with angles 90°, 45° and 45° is both right-angled and isosceles.

questionText: Meera has a thin straw 12 cm long. She cuts it into three pieces, each a whole number of centimetres long, and joins the pieces end to end to make a triangle. How many different triangles can she make? (Triangles with the same three side lengths count as one.)
hints: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter ones together are longer than the longest one. List the ways to split the straw in an orderly way and test each.
The longest piece must be shorter than half of 12 cm, so it can be at most 5 cm. Start with a longest piece of 5 cm and find the other two.

Similar problem: a 10 cm straw. The longest piece must be less than 5 cm, so try 4 cm: the other two add up to 6 cm, giving 2, 4, 4 and 3, 3, 4. A longest piece of 3 cm would need the others to add up to 7 cm, which is too much. So a 10 cm straw gives 2 triangles.

stepByStep.text: The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side, so the longest side is less than 6 cm.
Longest side 5 cm: the other two add up to 7 cm. They can be 2 cm and 5 cm, or 3 cm and 4 cm.
Longest side 4 cm: the other two add up to 8 cm, so they must be 4 cm and 4 cm.
A longest side of 3 cm or less cannot reach a total of 12 cm.
So Meera can make 3 different triangles.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Only 2, 5, 5 and 3, 4, 5 and 4, 4, 4 close up into a triangle, which makes 3.
misconceptions.B: This counts every way to split 12 into three pieces. Many of them, like 1, 1, 10, cannot close up into a triangle. Test each split.
misconceptions.C: This also counts 1, 5, 6 and 2, 4, 6 and 3, 3, 6. In those, the two short pieces only just reach along the long one and lie flat. They need to be longer.
misconceptions.D: Good try! Check your list once more: one of your four may have two short pieces that add up to exactly the long piece.

questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 11 cm long. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. How many different lengths can the third side have?
hints: The third side cannot be too short or too long. Find the shortest and the longest whole number it can be, then count carefully.
The third side must be longer than 11 - 6 and shorter than 11 + 6. Decide whether those two end numbers themselves are allowed.
Similar problem: sides of 4 cm and 9 cm. The third side must be more than 5 cm and less than 13 cm, so it can be 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12 cm. That is 7 different lengths.

stepByStep.text: The third side must be longer than the difference of the other two.
The third side must be shorter than the sum of the other two.
A side of exactly 5 cm or exactly 17 cm would make the three sides lie flat, so the third side can be 6 cm up to 16 cm.
Count the whole numbers from 6 to 16.
So the third side can have 11 different lengths.

misconceptions.A: This counts 5 cm and 17 cm too. With those lengths the sides lie flat in a line and no triangle is made.
misconceptions.B: This is 17 - 5. Subtracting does not count the whole numbers strictly between 5 and 17. Try listing them.
misconceptions.C: Almost! Count again from 6 up to 16, pointing at each number once.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The third side can be any whole number from 6 cm to 16 cm, and that is 11 lengths.

questionText: In an isosceles triangle, one angle is 4 times another angle. The triangle has no obtuse angle. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The equal angles could be the two small ones or the two big ones. Try both and see which fits everything the question says.
Call the small angle one part. Then the angles are either 1, 1 and 4 parts, or 1, 4 and 4 parts. All the parts together make 180°.

Similar problem: in an isosceles triangle one angle is 2 times another and no angle is a right angle. Parts 1, 1, 2 give 45°, 45°, 90°, which has a right angle. Parts 1, 2, 2 give 5 parts = 180°, so one part is 36°. The smallest angle is 36°.

stepByStep.text: First case: the two equal angles are the small ones. The parts are 1, 1 and 4.
That gives 30°, 30° and 120°. But 120° is obtuse, so this case is not allowed.
Second case: the two equal angles are the big ones. The parts are 1, 4 and 4.
That gives 20°, 80° and 80°. No angle is obtuse, so this is the triangle.
So the smallest angle is 20°.

misconceptions.A: This comes from angles of 30°, 30° and 120°. Look at the 120°: the question says there is no obtuse angle. Try the other case.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! The angles are 20°, 80° and 80°: one is 4 times another and none is obtuse.
misconceptions.C: This divides 180° by 5, as if there were only two angles. A triangle has three angles, and two of them are equal.
misconceptions.D: With 45° the equal angles would be 45° and 45°, leaving 90°. Is any angle then 4 times another? Try using parts.

questionText: Two triangles are both isosceles, and each of them has an angle of 40°. The two triangles do not have the same set of angles. What is the difference between the largest angle of one triangle and the largest angle of the other?
hints: In an isosceles triangle, a given angle can be one of the two equal angles, or it can be the angle that is different. That gives two different triangles.
First let 40° be one of the two equal angles and find the third angle. Then let 40° be the different angle and find the two equal ones.

Similar problem with 20°: if 20° is one of the equal angles, the angles are 20°, 20°, 140°. If 20° is the different angle, the others are 80° each. The largest angles are 140° and 80°, and their difference is 60°.

stepByStep.text: If 40° is one of the two equal angles, the third angle is what is left from 180°.
If 40° is the different angle, the two equal angles share what is left.
So the triangles have angles 40°, 40°, 100° and 40°, 70°, 70°.
Subtract the two largest angles.
So the difference between the two largest angles is 30°.

misconceptions.A: This is 100° - 40°, the difference inside one triangle. The question asks about the largest angle of each of the two triangles.
misconceptions.B: 100° is the largest angle of one triangle. Now find the largest angle of the other triangle and subtract.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The largest angles are 100° and 70°, and 100 - 70 = 30.
misconceptions.D: 70° is the largest angle of one triangle. Find the largest angle of the other one and take the difference.

questionText: An isosceles triangle has one side of 5 cm and another side of 11 cm. What is its perimeter?
hints: The third side must be equal to one of the two sides you know. Try each choice, and check that the three sides can really make a triangle.
If the third side is 5 cm, the sides are 5, 5 and 11. Add the two short sides and compare with the long side.
Similar problem: an isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm and 9 cm. Sides 4, 4, 9 cannot meet because 4 + 4 is less than 9. Sides 4, 9, 9 can. The perimeter is 4 + 9 + 9 = 22 cm.

stepByStep.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, so the third side is either 5 cm or 11 cm.
Try 5 cm: the two short sides together must be longer than the longest side.
10 cm is shorter than 11 cm, so sides of 5, 5 and 11 cannot make a triangle.
So the third side is 11 cm. Add the three sides.
So the perimeter is 27 cm.

misconceptions.A: Exactly right! The sides must be 5 cm, 11 cm and 11 cm, which add up to 27 cm.
misconceptions.B: This uses sides 5, 5 and 11. Try to picture it: the two 5 cm sides together are only 10 cm, so they cannot reach across the 11 cm side.
misconceptions.C: This adds only the two sides given. A triangle has three sides, so find the third one first.
misconceptions.D: This adds 5 + 5 + 11 + 11, which is four sides. A triangle has only three. Decide which length is repeated.

questionText: Aman has a big box of sticks. Every stick is 3 cm, 4 cm or 8 cm long, and there are plenty of each length. He makes a triangle using three sticks as its three sides. The sticks may have the same length. How many different triangles can he make?
hints: List every way to choose three lengths: all the same, two the same, and all different. Then test each choice to see whether it can really make a triangle.
Start with the three choices where all sticks are equal. Then take two equal sticks with one different stick, and check that the two shorter sticks together are longer than the longest.
Similar problem: sticks of 2 cm and 5 cm only. The choices are 2, 2, 2 and 5, 5, 5 and 2, 2, 5 and 2, 5, 5. In 2, 2, 5 the short sticks add up to only 4 cm, so it is out. That leaves 3 triangles.

stepByStep.text: All three sticks equal: 3, 3, 3 and 4, 4, 4 and 8, 8, 8. All three make triangles.
Two equal and one different: 3, 3, 4 and 3, 4, 4 and 3, 8, 8 and 4, 8, 8 make triangles.
But 3, 3, 8 and 4, 4, 8 do not, because the two short sticks are not longer than the long one.
All different: 3, 4, 8 does not make a triangle either.
Count the choices that are left.
So Aman can make 7 different triangles.

misconceptions.A: Lovely work! Three equal-sided triangles and four with two equal sides make 7.
misconceptions.B: This counts every choice of three sticks. Test 3, 3, 8 and 3, 4, 8 and 4, 4, 8: can the short sticks reach across the 8 cm stick?
misconceptions.C: Nearly there! Look again at 4, 4, 8. The two 4 cm sticks add up to exactly 8 cm, so they lie flat along the long stick.
misconceptions.D: These are only the triangles with three equal sticks. Aman may also mix lengths, such as 3, 3, 4.

questionText: The three angles of a triangle are whole numbers of degrees, and all three are different. What is the largest size the smallest angle can have?
hints: To make the smallest angle as big as possible, the three angles should be as close to each other as they can be while staying different.
If all three were equal they would be 60° each. They must be different, so think about three whole numbers very close to 60 that add up to 180.
Similar problem: three different whole numbers add up to 30. Equal shares would be 10 each. The closest different numbers are 9, 10 and 11, so the smallest can be at most 9.

stepByStep.text: If the three angles were equal, each would be 60°.
The angles must be different, so the smallest must be less than 60°.
Try 59° for the smallest. The other two must add up to 121°, and 60° and 61° do that.
So the largest size the smallest angle can have is 59°.

misconceptions.A: A smallest angle of 60° would force all three angles to be 60°. The question says all three are different.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Angles of 59°, 60° and 61° are all different and add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: Angles like 58°, 60° and 62° do fit, but the smallest can be a little bigger than this. Try 59°.
misconceptions.D: If the smallest angle were 89°, the other two would each be at least 90°, and the total would pass 180°.

questionText: Which of these statements is true for every triangle?

options.text: Its largest angle is more than 60°
It has at least two acute angles
Its two smallest angles add up to less than 90°
Exactly one of its angles is 60° or more

hints: A statement is true for every triangle only if no triangle at all breaks it. For each statement, try to think of a triangle that breaks it.
Test each statement on some special triangles: the equilateral triangle, a right-angled triangle, and an isosceles triangle with angles 40°, 70°, 70°.

Similar problem: is 'every triangle has an angle of less than 60°' always true? Test the equilateral triangle: its angles are 60°, 60°, 60°, and none is less than 60°. One triangle that breaks the statement is enough, so it is not always true.

stepByStep.text: The equilateral triangle has angles 60°, 60°, 60°. Its largest angle is not more than 60°, and its two smallest angles add up to 120°.
A triangle with angles 40°, 70°, 70° has two angles of 60° or more, not exactly one.
Could a triangle have two angles that are not acute? Two angles of 90° or more already use up the whole 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle.
So at most one angle can be right or obtuse, and the other two must be acute.
The statement true for every triangle is: it has at least two acute angles.

misconceptions.A: This is true for almost every triangle. Check the equilateral triangle: its largest angle is exactly 60°, not more.
misconceptions.B: Well reasoned! Two angles of 90° or more would leave nothing for the third angle, so two angles are always acute.
misconceptions.C: This holds for obtuse-angled triangles only. Try 60°, 60°, 60°: the two smallest angles add up to 120°.
misconceptions.D: Try a triangle with angles 40°, 70° and 70°. How many of its angles are 60° or more?

questionText: Five equilateral triangles, each with sides of 4 cm, are placed in a row. The first points up, the second points down, the third points up, and so on. Each triangle shares one whole side with the next triangle, so together they make one flat shape with no gaps. What is the perimeter of this shape?
hints: The perimeter is only the outside edge. Every side that two triangles share is inside the shape, and it is hidden for both of those triangles.
Count how many sides are shared between neighbours in a row of five triangles. Each shared side removes one side from each of two triangles.

Similar problem: three equilateral triangles of side 5 cm in a row. All sides together make 9 sides. There are 2 shared sides, and each hides 2 sides, so 9 - 4 = 5 sides stay outside. The perimeter is 5 x 5 = 25 cm.

stepByStep.text: Five separate triangles have 15 sides in all.
In a row of five triangles there are 4 places where two neighbours share a side.
Each shared side hides one side of each neighbour, so 8 sides are hidden.
Count the sides left on the outside and multiply by 4 cm.
So the perimeter of the shape is 28 cm.

misconceptions.A: This is the total of all five separate perimeters. Once the triangles are joined, the shared sides are inside the shape.
misconceptions.B: Good try! This takes away each shared side once. A shared side belongs to two triangles, so it must come off twice.
misconceptions.C: This takes away one side too few. Count again: 15 sides in all, and 8 of them are hidden inside.
misconceptions.D: Wonderful! Seven sides of 4 cm stay on the outside, and 7 x 4 = 28.

questionText: The sides of a triangle are three consecutive whole numbers of centimetres, such as 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. What is the smallest perimeter such a triangle can have?
hints: Start from the smallest consecutive numbers, but check each time that the three lengths can really close up into a triangle.
Try 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm first. Add the two shorter sides and compare the total with the longest side.

Similar problem: the sides are three consecutive even numbers. Try 2, 4, 6: 2 + 4 is only equal to 6, so they lie flat. Try 4, 6, 8: 4 + 6 = 10 is more than 8, so it is a triangle. The smallest perimeter is 4 + 6 + 8 = 18 cm.

stepByStep.text: Try the smallest set, 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm. The two shorter sides only equal the longest side, so they lie flat.
Try the next set, 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. The two shorter sides are longer than the longest side.
So 2, 3, 4 is the smallest such triangle. Add its sides.
So the smallest perimeter is 9 cm.

misconceptions.A: This is 1 + 2 + 3. Check those sides: 1 cm and 2 cm together only just reach along the 3 cm side, so no triangle is made.
misconceptions.B: Sides of 3, 4 and 5 cm do make a triangle, but there is a smaller set that works too. Try 2, 3, 4.
misconceptions.C: A perimeter of 3 cm would need sides of 1, 1 and 1 cm, and those are not consecutive numbers.
misconceptions.D: Spot on! 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm is the smallest set that closes up, and 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.

questionText: The perimeter of a triangle is 30 cm, and each side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the greatest length its longest side can have?
hints: The longest side cannot take too much of the perimeter. The other two sides together must still be longer than it.
Suppose the longest side is 15 cm. Work out what is left for the other two sides together, and compare.

Similar problem: perimeter 20 cm. If the longest side were 10 cm, the other two would add up to 10 cm and lie flat. With 9 cm, the other two add up to 11 cm, which is more. So the greatest longest side is 9 cm.

stepByStep.text: The other two sides together must be longer than the longest side.
Try 15 cm. The other two sides add up to 15 cm, which is only equal, so they lie flat.
Try 14 cm. The other two sides add up to 16 cm, which is more than 14 cm.
Sides such as 14 cm, 14 cm and 2 cm make a real triangle.
So the greatest length of the longest side is 14 cm.

misconceptions.A: This leaves only 1 cm and 1 cm for the other sides. Two tiny sides cannot reach across a 28 cm side.
misconceptions.B: Yes! With 14 cm, the other two sides share 16 cm, which is just enough to close the triangle.
misconceptions.C: So close! With 15 cm, the other two sides add up to exactly 15 cm. They need to be longer than the longest side.
misconceptions.D: 10 cm is the side of the equilateral triangle. The longest side can be made bigger than that. How big, before the others cannot reach?

questionText: A triangle is right-angled. One of its angles is 4 times another of its angles, and all three angles are whole numbers of degrees. What is the smallest angle of the triangle?
hints: One angle is 90°. Decide which two angles are in the '4 times' relation: could the right angle be one of them? Use the clue about whole numbers.
If 90° were 4 times another angle, that angle would be 90 ÷ 4. Check whether that is a whole number. If not, the relation is between the two acute angles.

Similar problem: in a right-angled triangle, one acute angle is 5 times the other acute angle. The two acute angles add up to 90°, and they make 6 equal parts. One part is 90 ÷ 6 = 15°, so the angles are 15°, 75° and 90°.

stepByStep.text: If the right angle were 4 times another angle, that angle would not be a whole number.
So the relation is between the two acute angles. Together they make 90°.
One acute angle is 1 part and the other is 4 parts, 5 parts in all.
The angles are 18°, 72° and 90°.
So the smallest angle is 18°.

misconceptions.A: Excellent! The acute angles are 18° and 72°, and 72 is 4 times 18.
misconceptions.B: This is 90° divided by 4. The question says every angle is a whole number of degrees, so the right angle is not the one that is 4 times another.
misconceptions.C: This divides the full 180° into 5 parts. One angle is already 90°, so only the other 90° is shared between the two acute angles.
misconceptions.D: 72° is one of the angles, but it is the bigger acute angle. The question asks for the smallest angle.

questionText: Two sides of a triangle are 9 cm and 4 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres, and the perimeter of the triangle is a multiple of 7. How long is the third side?
hints: Two things must both be true: the three sides must be able to make a triangle, and the perimeter must be in the 7 times table. Find the possible third sides first.
The third side must be more than 9 - 4 and less than 9 + 4. For each allowed length, the perimeter is 13 plus that length.

Similar problem: sides 5 cm and 8 cm, perimeter a multiple of 10. The third side is between 3 cm and 13 cm, so the perimeter is between 16 cm and 26 cm. The only multiple of 10 there is 20, so the third side is 20 - 13 = 7 cm.

stepByStep.text: The third side must be more than 5 cm and less than 13 cm.
So the third side is from 6 cm to 12 cm, and the perimeter is from 19 cm to 25 cm.
The only multiple of 7 from 19 to 25 is 21.
Take away the two known sides.
So the third side is 8 cm.

misconceptions.A: A 1 cm side gives a perimeter of 14 cm, which is a multiple of 7. But can 1 cm and 4 cm together reach across the 9 cm side?
misconceptions.B: A 15 cm side gives a perimeter of 28 cm. But 9 cm and 4 cm together are only 13 cm, too short to meet across 15 cm.
misconceptions.C: Super! Sides of 9, 4 and 8 cm make a triangle, and the perimeter is 21 cm, which is 7 x 3.
misconceptions.D: The perimeter must be a multiple of 7, not the side itself. With a 7 cm side the perimeter would be 20 cm.

questionText: Triangle ABC is isosceles. Angle A is 50°. Angle B is bigger than angle A and also bigger than angle C. What is angle C?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The clues about angle B tell you which two angles make the equal pair.
Angle B is bigger than each of the other two angles, so it cannot be equal to either of them. Which two angles are left to be the equal pair?

Here is a similar one: triangle PQR is isosceles, angle P is 35°, and angle Q is bigger than both other angles. Angle Q cannot be in the equal pair, so angle R equals angle P, which is 35°. Then angle Q is 180° − 35° − 35° = 110°.

stepByStep.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles.
Angle B is bigger than angle A and bigger than angle C, so it is not equal to either of them. The equal pair must be angle A and angle C.
Check that this fits: angle B would be 180° − 50° − 50° = 80°, which is bigger than 50°.
So angle C is equal to angle A, and angle C is 50°.

misconceptions.A: 65° comes from sharing 180° − 50° = 130° equally between angles B and C. But angle B is bigger than angle C, so those two cannot be equal.
misconceptions.B: 80° is the size of the biggest angle, angle B. The question asks for angle C, which is one of the equal pair.
misconceptions.C: 130° is what angles B and C make together, 180° − 50°. Angle C is only one of those two angles.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Angle B is the odd one out, so angles A and C are the equal pair and angle C is 50°, the same as angle A.

questionText: Two angles of a triangle add up to 110°. The bigger of these two angles is 30° more than the smaller one. What kind of triangle is it?
hints: To name a triangle you need all three angles. Find the two angles described, then do not forget the third one.
Take the extra 30° away from 110°. What is left is twice the smaller angle.

Similar problem: two angles add up to 100° and differ by 20°. Taking 20 from 100 leaves 80, so the smaller is 40° and the bigger is 60°. The third angle is 180 - 100 = 80°. All three are different, so that triangle is scalene.

stepByStep.text: Take away the extra 30°. What is left is two equal shares.
So the two angles are 40° and 70°.
Find the third angle.
The angles are 40°, 70° and 70°. Two of them are equal.
So it is an isosceles triangle.

misconceptions.A: The two angles described, 70° and 40°, are different. Now find the third angle and compare it with them.
misconceptions.B: A right-angled triangle needs an angle of 90°. Work out all three angles and check.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The angles are 40°, 70° and 70°, and two equal angles make the triangle isosceles.
misconceptions.D: An equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°. Here the two angles described differ by 30°.

questionText: In a triangle, two angles are 41° and 40°. Find the third angle.
hints: All three angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
Add the two known angles: 41 + 40 = 81.
Subtract from 180: 180 − 81 = ?

stepByStep.text: Angles of a triangle sum to 180°.

misconceptions.A: An angle can never be less than zero. Think about what the three angles of a triangle add up to.
misconceptions.B: 279 is 360 − 81, which uses a full turn. The three angles of a triangle make only 180° together.
misconceptions.C: That's it! 41 + 40 = 81, and the third angle is what is left of 180°: 180 − 81 = 99.
misconceptions.D: 81 is 41 + 40, the two angles you know added together. Now find what is left of 180°.

questionText: Angles of a triangle are in the ratio 3:1:1. Find the largest angle.
hints: Add ratio parts: 3+1+1 = 5.
Divide 180 by 5 to find one part.
Multiply the largest ratio number by one part.

stepByStep.text: Sum of ratio parts = 5

misconceptions.A: 36 is 180 ÷ 5, the size of one part. The largest angle has more than one part, so there is one more step.
misconceptions.B: 60 is 180 ÷ 3, which gives all three angles the same size. The ratio 3:1:1 says they are not equal, so count the parts first.
misconceptions.C: Yes! There are 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 parts, so one part is 180 ÷ 5 = 36°. The largest angle is 3 × 36 = 108°.
misconceptions.D: 109 is just a little off. Check your last multiplying step once more, ones first.

questionText: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 4 cm.
hints: This is an area of a triangle problem. A triangle covers half the space of a rectangle that has the same base and height.
First multiply the base by the height, 12 × 4. Then remember that the triangle is only half of that rectangle.
Here is a similar problem: a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm. Base times height is 10 × 6 = 60. Half of 60 is 30, so the area is 30 square cm.

stepByStep.text: The area of a triangle is half of its base times its height.
Base times height is 12 × 4 = 48.
Half of 48 is 24. So the area is 24 square cm.

misconceptions.A: 16 comes from adding the base and the height, 12 + 4. For area we multiply them and then take half.
misconceptions.B: 96 comes from doubling 12 × 4 when it should be halved. A triangle is half of the rectangle.
misconceptions.C: Great job! 12 × 4 = 48, and half of 48 is 24.
misconceptions.D: 48 is 12 × 4, the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of that.

questionText: In a triangle, two angles are 30° and 37°. Find the third angle.
hints: All three angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
Add the two known angles: 30 + 37 = 67.
Subtract from 180: 180 − 67 = ?

stepByStep.text: Angles of a triangle sum to 180°.

misconceptions.A: This number is below zero, and no angle can be smaller than zero. The third angle is the rest of the triangle's angle total.
misconceptions.B: 67 is 30 + 37, the two angles you know added together. Now find what is left of 180°.
misconceptions.C: That's it! 30 + 37 = 67, and the third angle is what is left of 180°: 180 − 67 = 113.
misconceptions.D: 293 is 360 − 67. The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, not 360°.

questionText: In a triangle, two angles are 76° and 58°. Find the third angle.
hints: All three angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
Add the two known angles: 76 + 58 = 134.
Subtract from 180: 180 − 134 = ?

stepByStep.text: Angles of a triangle sum to 180°.

misconceptions.A: 44 is too small. Check by adding: 76 + 58 + 44 = 178, which is short of what a triangle's angles make.
misconceptions.B: 134 is 76 + 58. That is a good first step. The third angle is the rest of the triangle's 180°.
misconceptions.C: 226 is 360 − 134, which uses a full turn. The three angles of a triangle make only 180° together.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The three angles add up to 180°. 76 + 58 = 134, and 180 − 134 = 46.

questionText: Angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1:1:4. Find the largest angle.
hints: Add ratio parts: 1+1+4 = 6.
Divide 180 by 6 to find one part.
Multiply the largest ratio number by one part.

stepByStep.text: Sum of ratio parts = 6

misconceptions.A: 30 is 180 ÷ 6, the size of one part. The largest angle has more than one part, so there is one more step.
misconceptions.B: 60 is 180 ÷ 3. That shares the 180° equally, but the ratio 1:1:4 gives the angles different numbers of parts.
