Here is a similar problem. Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°. Together they make 50 + 70 = 120°. The third angle is 180 − 120 = 60°.

stepByStep.text: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
The two known angles add up to 35 + 65 = 100°.
The third angle is what is left: 180 − 100 = 80. So the third angle is 80°.

misconceptions.B: With 110° the three angles would add up to 210°, which is too much. Add the two known angles first, then take the sum from 180°.
misconceptions.C: With 90° the three angles would add up to 190°, a little more than 180°. Take the sum of the two known angles from 180°.
misconceptions.D: 100° is the sum of the two known angles, 35 + 65. Take that away from 180° to find the third angle.

questionText: Two angles of a triangle are 52° and 59°. What is the third angle?
hints: Every triangle's three angles make 180° altogether. You know two of them, so the third is whatever is left over.
First add the two angles you know, 52° and 59°. Then think about how far that total is from 180°.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 20° and 95°. 20 + 95 = 115, and 180 − 115 = 65. The third angle is 65°.

stepByStep.text: Add the two angles you know.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Take the total away from 180°. The third angle is 69°.

misconceptions.A: This is 10° too big. The two angles add up to 111°, so take 111 from 180 once more.
misconceptions.C: This adds 111 to 180. The three angles share 180° between them, so take 111 away from 180 instead.
misconceptions.D: This is 10° too small. The two angles add up to 111°, so take 111 from 180 once more.

questionText: If two angles of a triangle are 28° and 45°, what type of triangle is it?
hints: This asks you to name a triangle by its angles. A triangle is acute-angled if all its angles are less than 90°, right-angled if one angle is exactly 90°, and obtuse-angled if one angle is more than 90°. You need all three angles to decide.
The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. First find the third angle by adding 28° and 45° and taking the sum away from 180°.

Here is a similar problem. Two angles of a triangle are 60° and 50°. Together they make 110°, so the third angle is 180 − 110 = 70°. All three angles are less than 90°, so that triangle is acute-angled.

stepByStep.text: The two known angles add up to 28 + 45 = 73°.
The three angles add up to 180°, so the third angle is 180 − 73 = 107°.
107° is more than 90°, so it is an obtuse angle.
A triangle with one obtuse angle is an obtuse-angled triangle.

misconceptions.A: The two given angles are acute, but the third angle must be checked too. It is 107°, which is more than 90°.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The third angle is 107°, which is more than 90°, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
misconceptions.C: An isosceles triangle needs two equal angles. The angles here are 28°, 45° and 107°, which are all different.
misconceptions.D: Two angles are enough, because the third can be found by taking their sum away from 180°. Find it and see how big it is.

questionText: Which of the following can be the lengths of the sides of a triangle?
hints: This is about which three lengths can make a triangle. The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side, or they cannot meet.
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the sum with the longest length. Start with 2 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm.

Here is a similar problem. Can 3 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm make a triangle? 3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 9, so they cannot. Can 4 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm make a triangle? 4 + 7 = 11, which is more than 10, so they can.

stepByStep.text: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter sides together are longer than the longest side.
For 2 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm: 2 + 5 = 7, which is less than 9, so the short sides cannot meet.
For 1 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm: 1 + 5 = 6, which is only equal to the longest side, so the short sides would lie flat along it.
For 6 cm, 8 cm and 12 cm: 6 + 8 = 14, which is more than 12. So the lengths that can make a triangle are 6 cm, 8 cm and 12 cm.

misconceptions.A: Here 2 + 5 = 7, which is shorter than 9, so the two short sides cannot reach each other. Look for a set where the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest.
misconceptions.B: You got it! 6 + 8 = 14 is more than 12, so these three sides can meet to make a triangle.
misconceptions.C: Here 1 + 5 = 6, exactly the same as the longest side, so the short sides would lie flat along it. The sum must be more than the longest side.
misconceptions.D: Not every set here can make a triangle. Test each one by adding the two shorter sides and comparing with the longest.

questionText: Which of the following are the measures of the angles of an isosceles triangle?
hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and so it also has two equal angles. Look for a set of angles with a matching pair.
Go through each set and see whether any angle appears twice. Start with 30°, 60° and 90°.

Here is a similar problem. Which is isosceles: a triangle with angles 50°, 60°, 70° or one with angles 40°, 40°, 100°? The first has three different angles. The second has two angles of 40°, and 40 + 40 + 100 = 180, so the second one is isosceles.

stepByStep.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles.
In 30°, 60°, 90°, in 40°, 120°, 20° and in 50°, 90°, 40°, all three angles are different.
In the remaining set two angles are both 75°, and the three angles add up to 180°.
So the angles of an isosceles triangle are 30°, 75°, 75°.

misconceptions.A: 30°, 60° and 90° are all different, so this triangle is scalene. Look for a set with two equal angles.
misconceptions.B: 40°, 120° and 20° are all different, so this triangle is scalene. Look for a set with two equal angles.
misconceptions.C: 50°, 90° and 40° are all different, so this triangle is scalene. Look for a set with two equal angles.
misconceptions.D: Great job! Two of the angles are both 75°, and that matching pair makes the triangle isosceles.

questionText: Two angles of a triangle are 61° and 26°. What is the third angle?
hints: This uses the angle sum of a triangle: the three angles together make 180°. Find the part that is missing.
First add the two angles you know, 61° and 26°. Then think about how far that total is from 180°.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 48° and 62°. 48 + 62 = 110, and 180 − 110 = 70. The third angle is 70°.

stepByStep.text: Add the two angles you know.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Take the total away from 180°. The third angle is 93°.

misconceptions.A: This adds 87 to 180. The three angles share 180° between them, so take 87 away from 180 instead.
misconceptions.C: This is 10° too big. The two angles add up to 87°, so take 87 from 180 once more.
misconceptions.D: This is 10° too small. The two angles add up to 87°, so take 87 from 180 once more.

questionText: One acute angle of a right-angled triangle measures 27°. What is the other acute angle?
hints: This is a missing-angle problem in a right-angled triangle. One angle is 90°, and the three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Since one angle is 90°, the two acute angles share the other 90° between them. Take the acute angle you know away from 90°.
Here is a similar problem. One acute angle of a right-angled triangle is 35°. The two acute angles add up to 90°, so the other is 90 − 35 = 55°. Check: 90 + 35 + 55 = 180.

stepByStep.text: A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90°. The three angles add up to 180°, so the two acute angles together make 180 − 90 = 90°.
One acute angle is 27°, so the other is 90 − 27 = 63.
So the other acute angle is 63°.

misconceptions.A: 73° is 10° too big: 27 + 73 = 100, but the two acute angles must add up to 90°. Try the subtraction 90 − 27 again.
misconceptions.B: Well done! The two acute angles add up to 90°, and 90 − 27 = 63°.
misconceptions.C: The two acute angles are equal only when each is 45°. Here they must add up to 90°, so find 90 − 27.
misconceptions.D: 90° is the right angle itself. The question asks for the other acute angle, which is less than 90°.

questionText: Two angles of a triangle are 52° and 73°. What is the third angle?
hints: The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°. Two are given, so find what is left for the third.
First add the two angles you know, 52° and 73°. Then think about how far that total is from 180°.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 33° and 57°. 33 + 57 = 90, and 180 − 90 = 90. The third angle is 90°.

stepByStep.text: Add the two angles you know.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Take the total away from 180°. The third angle is 55°.

misconceptions.B: This is 10° too big. The two angles add up to 125°, so take 125 from 180 once more.
misconceptions.C: This adds 125 to 180. The three angles share 180° between them, so take 125 away from 180 instead.
misconceptions.D: This is 10° too small. The two angles add up to 125°, so take 125 from 180 once more.

questionText: In a right-angled isosceles triangle, each of the equal angles measures:
hints: This triangle is both right-angled and isosceles. So one angle is 90° and the other two angles are equal.
The three angles add up to 180°. First take away the right angle to find what the two equal angles share.
Here is a similar problem. An isosceles triangle has one angle of 110° and two equal angles. The two equal angles share 180 − 110 = 70°, so each one is 70 ÷ 2 = 35°.

stepByStep.text: One angle is 90°. The three angles add up to 180°, so the other two together make 180 − 90 = 90°.
The other two angles are equal, so each is half of 90°.
So each of the equal angles measures 45°.

misconceptions.A: 90° is the right angle. Two angles of 90° would use up all 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle.
misconceptions.B: Excellent thinking! The two equal angles share 90°, so each is 45°.
misconceptions.C: 60° is each angle of an equilateral triangle. Here one angle is 90°, so the other two share only 90°.
misconceptions.D: Two angles of 40° with 90° add up to 170°, which is 10° short. Share the remaining 90° equally.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a type of triangle?
questionLatex: \text{Which is NOT a valid triangle type?}
hints: Each name joins two ideas: one about the angles and one about the sides. Look for the name where the two ideas cannot both be true in the same triangle.
Think about an equilateral triangle. All three of its angles are equal, so work out what each one must be. Could one of them be a right angle?

Here is a similar one: can there be an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle? The three equal angles of an equilateral triangle are each 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. An obtuse angle is more than 90°, so an angle of 60° cannot be obtuse. Such a triangle cannot exist.

stepByStep.text: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. In an equilateral triangle all three are equal, so each is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
A right-angled triangle must have one angle of 90°. An angle cannot be 60° and 90° at once.
The other three names are possible. For example, 70°, 70°, 40° is acute-angled isosceles, 100°, 40°, 40° is obtuse-angled isosceles, and 50°, 60°, 70° is acute-angled scalene.
So the one that is not a type of triangle is the right-angled equilateral triangle.

misconceptions.A: This triangle can be drawn. Angles of 70°, 70° and 40° are all less than 90°, and two of them are equal.
misconceptions.B: This triangle can be drawn. Angles of 100°, 40° and 40° have one angle bigger than 90° and two equal angles.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°, so it can never have a right angle.
misconceptions.D: This triangle can be drawn. Angles of 50°, 60° and 70° are all less than 90° and all different.

questionText: Which of the following are the angles of an obtuse-angled scalene triangle?
hints: Two things must both be true here. Obtuse-angled means one angle is more than 90°, and scalene means all three angles are different.
First set aside any set that has no angle bigger than 90°. Then, in the sets that are left, see whether all three angles are different.

Here is a similar problem. Which is an acute-angled isosceles triangle: 70°, 70°, 40° or 100°, 40°, 40°? Both have two equal angles, so both are isosceles. Only in the first are all the angles less than 90°, so 70°, 70°, 40° is the acute-angled isosceles triangle.

stepByStep.text: An obtuse-angled triangle has one angle more than 90°. A scalene triangle has three different angles.
The sets 30°, 60°, 90° and 50°, 90°, 40° each have a largest angle of exactly 90°, so they are right-angled, not obtuse-angled.
The set 150°, 15°, 15° has an obtuse angle, but two of its angles are equal, so it is isosceles, not scalene.
In the last set, 120° is more than 90° and all three angles are different. So the obtuse-angled scalene triangle is 40°, 120°, 20°.

misconceptions.A: 30°, 60° and 90° are all different, so this triangle is scalene. But its biggest angle is exactly 90°, a right angle, and obtuse means more than 90°.
misconceptions.B: In 50°, 90° and 40° the biggest angle is 90°, which makes the triangle right-angled. Look for a set with an angle bigger than 90°.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 120° is more than 90°, and 40°, 120° and 20° are all different, so it is obtuse-angled and scalene.
misconceptions.D: This set does have an obtuse angle, 150°. But two of its angles are both 15°, which makes it isosceles, and scalene needs three different angles.

questionText: In a triangle, two interior angles are 55° and 70°. What is the exterior angle adjacent to the third angle?
hints: This is about an exterior angle of a triangle. An exterior angle and the interior angle next to it lie on a straight line, so together they make 180°.
First find the third interior angle. The three interior angles add up to 180°, so take 55° and 70° away from 180°.

Here is a similar problem. Two interior angles of a triangle are 40° and 60°. The third interior angle is 180 − 40 − 60 = 80°. The exterior angle next to it is 180 − 80 = 100°. Notice that this is the same as 40 + 60.

stepByStep.text: The three interior angles add up to 180°, so the third interior angle is 180 − 55 − 70 = 55°.
The exterior angle and the third interior angle lie on a straight line, so together they make 180°.
180 − 55 = 125, which is the same as 55 + 70. So the exterior angle is 125°.

misconceptions.A: 180° is the total of the exterior angle and the interior angle beside it. Take the third interior angle away from 180°.
misconceptions.B: 55° is the third interior angle. The question asks for the exterior angle beside it, which is 180 − 55.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The third interior angle is 55°, and the exterior angle beside it is 180 − 55 = 125°.
misconceptions.D: 110° is 180 − 70, the exterior angle beside the 70° angle. The one asked for is beside the third angle, which is 55°.

questionText: An exterior angle of a triangle is 130°. One of the opposite interior angles is 50°. What is the other?
hints: This uses a fact about triangles: an exterior angle is equal to the sum of the two interior angles opposite it, the ones that are not next to it.
The two opposite interior angles add up to 130°. One of them is 50°, so think about what must be added to 50° to make 130°.
Here is a similar problem. An exterior angle of a triangle is 110°, and one of the opposite interior angles is 45°. The two opposite interior angles add up to 110°, so the other is 110 − 45 = 65°.

stepByStep.text: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. So those two angles add up to 130°.
One of them is 50°, so the other is 130 − 50 = 80.
Check: the interior angle beside the exterior angle is 180 − 130 = 50°, and 50 + 50 + 80 = 180. So the other angle is 80°.

misconceptions.A: 50° is the interior angle beside the exterior angle, 180 − 130. The question asks for the other opposite angle, which is 130 − 50.
misconceptions.B: With 50° and 60° the two opposite angles add up to 110°, not 130°. Find 130 − 50.
misconceptions.C: 130° is the exterior angle itself. It is shared between the two opposite interior angles, so take 50° away from it.
misconceptions.D: You got it! The two opposite interior angles add up to 130°, and 130 − 50 = 80°.

questionText: In an isosceles triangle, each base angle is 70°. What is the vertex angle?
hints: This is a missing-angle problem. An isosceles triangle has two equal base angles and one vertex angle, and the three angles add up to 180°.
Both base angles are 70°. First add the two base angles together.
Here is a similar problem. Each base angle of an isosceles triangle is 65°. The two base angles make 65 + 65 = 130°. The vertex angle is 180 − 130 = 50°.

stepByStep.text: The two base angles are 70° each, so together they make 70 + 70 = 140°.
The three angles add up to 180°, so the vertex angle is 180 − 140 = 40.
So the vertex angle is 40°.

misconceptions.A: That would make all three angles 70°, which add up to 210°. Take the two base angles away from 180°.
misconceptions.B: 110° comes from taking away only one base angle, 180 − 70. There are two base angles of 70° each.
misconceptions.C: With 80° the three angles would add up to 220°. The two base angles make 140°, so find 180 − 140.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The base angles make 140° together, and 180 − 140 = 40°.

questionText: Two angles of a triangle are 75° and 74°. What is the third angle?
hints: Every triangle's three angles make 180° altogether. You know two of them, so the third is whatever is left over.
First add the two angles you know, 75° and 74°. Then think about how far that total is from 180°.
Similar example: two angles of a triangle are 25° and 110°. 25 + 110 = 135, and 180 − 135 = 45. The third angle is 45°.

stepByStep.text: Add the two angles you know.
All three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Take the total away from 180°. The third angle is 31°.

misconceptions.A: This is 10° too big. The two angles add up to 149°, so take 149 from 180 once more.
misconceptions.B: This adds 149 to 180. The three angles share 180° between them, so take 149 away from 180 instead.
misconceptions.D: This is 10° too small. The two angles add up to 149°, so take 149 from 180 once more.

questionText: The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is 50°. Each base angle is:
hints: This is a missing-angle problem. An isosceles triangle has one vertex angle and two equal base angles, and the three angles add up to 180°.
First take the vertex angle of 50° away from 180° to find what the two base angles share.
Here is a similar problem. The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is 40°. The two base angles share 180 − 40 = 140°. They are equal, so each one is 140 ÷ 2 = 70°.

stepByStep.text: The three angles add up to 180°, so the two base angles together make 180 − 50 = 130°.
The base angles are equal, so each is half of 130°.
So each base angle is 65°.

misconceptions.A: 130° is what the two base angles make together, 180 − 50. Share it equally between the two.
misconceptions.B: Three angles of 50° add up to only 150°. Take 50° from 180° and share what is left between the two base angles.
misconceptions.C: Two angles of 55° with 50° add up to 160°, which is 20° short. Take 50 from 180 and halve what is left.
misconceptions.D: Great job! The base angles share 130° equally, so each is 65°.

questionText: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite to the right angle is called the:
hints: The sides of a right-angled triangle have special names. One of them does not touch the right angle at all, and it has a name of its own.
Picture a right-angled triangle. Two sides meet to make the right angle. Look at the third side, the one facing the right angle, which is also the longest side.

Here is a similar one: in a right-angled triangle, what do we call the two sides that meet at the right angle? When the triangle stands on one of them, that side is the base and the other one is the height.

stepByStep.text: In a right-angled triangle, two sides meet to make the right angle.
The third side lies opposite the right angle, and it is the longest side of the triangle.
This side is called the hypotenuse.

misconceptions.A: A median is a line from a corner to the middle of the opposite side. It is not one of the three sides.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The side facing the right angle is the longest side, and it is called the hypotenuse.
misconceptions.C: The base is one of the two sides that meet at the right angle. The question asks about the side facing the right angle.
misconceptions.D: The height stands straight up from the base, so it touches the right angle. Look for the side that does not touch it.

questionText: How many axes of symmetry does a scalene triangle have?
hints: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves of a shape match exactly. For a triangle, think about which sides would have to land on each other.
Remember what scalene means: all three sides have different lengths. Imagine folding the triangle through each corner and ask whether the two halves would match.

Here is a similar problem. How many axes of symmetry does a triangle with exactly two equal sides have? Folding through the corner where the two equal sides meet lays one equal side on the other, so that fold line is an axis of symmetry. A fold through either of the other corners would put a longer side on a shorter one. So it has 1 axis of symmetry.

stepByStep.text: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves match exactly.
In a triangle, a fold through a corner makes matching halves only when the two sides that meet at that corner are equal.
A scalene triangle has three different sides, so no two sides are equal and no fold gives matching halves. So a scalene triangle has 0 axes of symmetry.

misconceptions.A: Well done! With three different sides, no fold can make the two halves match.
misconceptions.B: One axis of symmetry belongs to an isosceles triangle, which has two equal sides. A scalene triangle has no equal sides.
misconceptions.C: Three axes of symmetry belong to an equilateral triangle, where all the sides are equal. In a scalene triangle all the sides are different.
misconceptions.D: Think about whether a scalene triangle has any equal sides that could fold onto each other. Without a pair of equal sides there is no fold line.

questionText: A triangle has sides 8 cm, 11 cm, and 15 cm. Its perimeter is:
hints: This is a perimeter problem. The perimeter of a shape is the total distance around it.
Add the three sides. Start with 8 + 11, then add 15 to that.
Here is a similar problem. A triangle has sides 6 cm, 9 cm and 13 cm. 6 + 9 = 15, and 15 + 13 = 28. Its perimeter is 28 cm.

stepByStep.text: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides.
First add two of the sides: 8 + 11 = 19.
Then add the third side: 19 + 15 = 34. So the perimeter is 34 cm.

misconceptions.A: 1320 comes from multiplying the three sides, 8 × 11 × 15. For perimeter we add the sides.
misconceptions.B: You got it! 8 + 11 + 15 = 34 cm.
misconceptions.C: 24 cm is 10 too few. Add again carefully: 8 + 11 = 19, and then add 15.
misconceptions.D: 44 cm is 10 too many. Add again carefully: 8 + 11 = 19, and then add 15.

questionText: The perimeter of a triangle is 36 cm. Two sides are 12 cm and 9 cm. What is the third side?
hints: This is a perimeter problem worked backwards. The perimeter is the total of all three sides, and you know two of them.
First add the two sides you know, 12 cm and 9 cm. The third side is whatever is still needed to reach 36 cm.
Here is a similar problem. The perimeter of a triangle is 40 cm and two sides are 14 cm and 10 cm. The two known sides add up to 14 + 10 = 24 cm. The third side is 40 − 24 = 16 cm.

stepByStep.text: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides, so the three sides add up to 36 cm.
The two known sides add up to 12 + 9 = 21 cm.
The third side is what is left: 36 − 21 = 15. So the third side is 15 cm.

misconceptions.A: 17 cm is a little too much: 12 + 9 + 17 = 38. Add the two known sides first, then take that from 36.
misconceptions.B: 21 cm is the sum of the two known sides, 12 + 9. Take it away from the perimeter of 36 cm.
misconceptions.C: 3 cm is the difference between the two known sides, 12 − 9. The three sides must add up to 36 cm.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 12 + 9 = 21, and 36 − 21 = 15 cm.

questionText: A right-angled triangle has legs of 6 cm and 8 cm. What is its area?
hints: This is an area problem for a right-angled triangle. The two legs meet at the right angle, so one is the base and the other is the height. The triangle is half of the rectangle made with them.
Multiply the two legs, 6 × 8, to get the area of the rectangle. Then remember that the triangle is half of it.
Here is a similar problem. A right-angled triangle has legs of 10 cm and 6 cm. The rectangle made with them has area 10 × 6 = 60 cm². The triangle is half of that, so its area is 30 cm².

stepByStep.text: The legs meet at the right angle, so one leg is the base and the other is the height.
Base times height is 6 × 8 = 48.
The triangle is half of that rectangle: 48 ÷ 2 = 24. So the area is 24 cm².

misconceptions.A: Great job! 6 × 8 = 48, and half of 48 is 24 cm².
misconceptions.B: 14 comes from adding the legs, 6 + 8. For area, multiply them and then take half.
misconceptions.C: 10 cm is the length of the third side of this triangle, not its area. Multiply the two legs and take half.
misconceptions.D: 48 cm² is 6 × 8, the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of that.

questionText: A median of a triangle is a line segment joining a vertex to the _______ of the opposite side.
hints: This is about the meaning of a word. The word median is related to the word middle.
Picture a line drawn from one corner of a triangle across to the opposite side. Think about which special point on that side would cut the side into two equal parts.
Here is an example. In triangle PQR, side QR is 10 cm long. The point M on QR is 5 cm from Q and 5 cm from R. The line from P to M is a median of the triangle, because M cuts QR into two equal parts.

stepByStep.text: A median starts at a vertex of the triangle and goes across to the opposite side.
It meets that side exactly in the middle, cutting it into two equal parts. The point in the middle of a side is called its midpoint.
So a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

misconceptions.A: A line to just any point of the opposite side is not always a median. A median goes to one special point, the one that cuts the side into two equal parts.
misconceptions.B: A side has no highest point that stays the same when the triangle is turned around. Look for the point that cuts the side into two equal parts.
misconceptions.C: Well done! A median goes to the midpoint, the point that cuts the opposite side into two equal parts.
misconceptions.D: The end points of the opposite side are the other two corners, so that line would just be a side of the triangle. A median goes to the middle of the side.

questionText: How many medians does a triangle have?
hints: A median joins a vertex of a triangle to the middle of the opposite side. Think about how many different vertices a median can start from.
Count the vertices of a triangle. One median can be drawn from each vertex.
Here is a similar problem. How many diagonals does a rectangle have? A diagonal joins two opposite corners. A rectangle has 4 corners, which make 2 pairs of opposite corners, so it has 2 diagonals.

stepByStep.text: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
A triangle has 3 vertices, and each vertex has exactly one opposite side, so each vertex gives one median.
So a triangle has 3 medians.

misconceptions.A: 6 counts each median twice. Each of the 3 vertices gives just one median.
misconceptions.B: Two medians come from two of the vertices. There is one more vertex, and it has a median too.
misconceptions.C: One median comes from one vertex. The other two vertices have medians as well.
misconceptions.D: You got it! One median from each of the 3 vertices makes 3 medians.

questionText: In a triangle with angles 40°, 60°, and 80°, which side is the longest?
hints: In a triangle, the sizes of the angles and the lengths of the sides go together. A wider angle opens out to a longer side across from it.
Find the biggest of the three angles, 40°, 60° and 80°. Then think about the side that lies across the triangle from that angle.
Here is a similar one: a triangle has angles 30°, 50° and 100°. The biggest angle is 100°, so the longest side is the one opposite 100°.

stepByStep.text: In any triangle, the longest side is opposite the biggest angle.
The angles are 40°, 60° and 80°, and the biggest is 80°.
So the longest side is the side opposite 80°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 80° is the biggest angle, and the longest side always lies opposite the biggest angle.
misconceptions.B: 40° is the smallest angle, so the side opposite it is the shortest. Look for the biggest angle.
misconceptions.C: The sides are all equal only when the three angles are all equal. Here the angles are 40°, 60° and 80°.
misconceptions.D: 60° is the middle angle, so the side opposite it is the middle length. The longest side faces a bigger angle.

questionText: Can a triangle have two right angles?

options.text: Yes, if it's a big triangle
Yes, in a right-angled isosceles triangle

questionText: A right-angled triangle has a base of 12 cm and area of 42 cm². What is its height?
hints: A right-angled triangle is exactly half of a rectangle with the same base and height. So its area is half of base × height.
Start by doubling the triangle's area. That gives the area of the whole rectangle with the same base and height.

Here is a similar one: a right-angled triangle has base 10 cm and area 40 cm². The rectangle is twice as big, 2 × 40 = 80 cm². Its height is 80 ÷ 10 = 8 cm, and the triangle has the same height, 8 cm.

So the rectangle with the same base and height has area 2 × 42 = 84 cm².
The rectangle's area is base × height, so 12 × height = 84. The height is 84 ÷ 12 = 7.
The height of the triangle is 7 cm.
